DOCUMENT:
Pricing Proposal: Weekend Rate Restructure
Harbourside Hotel, Revenue Management, April 2026

1. Proposal
From 1 June 2026 we propose to (a) raise the Best Available Rate (BAR) for Friday and Saturday nights from £145 to £165, and (b) introduce a two-night minimum for any stay that includes a Saturday night. Midweek rates are unchanged.

2. Context
Harbourside is a 112-room four-star hotel on the quay, with a leisure-led weekend business and a corporate-led midweek business. Our weekend BAR is £20 to £35 below the three comparable hotels in our competitive set, whose weekend rates currently range from £165 to £180. Weekend occupancy has recovered strongly since 2023 and we believe we are leaving money on the table.

Table 1. Weekend (Friday and Saturday) occupancy by month, 2025
Jan 62% | Feb 66% | Mar 74% | Apr 80% | May 85% | Jun 81%
Jul 89% | Aug 93% | Sep 88% | Oct 82% | Nov 72% | Dec 78%

Average weekend occupancy across 2025 was 79%. July and August are our strongest months, driven by the harbour festival and the school summer holidays, with September also benefiting from late-season visitors.

3. Evidence on price sensitivity
In the last week of June 2025 we raised the weekend BAR by £10, from £135 to the current £145. Weekend occupancy in July rose to 89%, from 81% in June. This tells us that our weekend guests are not price sensitive at current levels; if anything, the higher rate appears to have reinforced our positioning as a quality option, and we expect the further increase to be absorbed in the same way.

This is consistent with feedback from our guest satisfaction surveys, where weekend guests rate "value for money" at 8.4 out of 10, the highest score among our competitive set.

4. Two-night minimum
Saturday nights are our most constrained inventory: we sold out on 31 Saturdays in 2025. Many of these guests stay only one night, leaving rooms empty on Friday or Sunday either side. A two-night minimum for stays including a Saturday will convert single-night Saturday stays into two-night stays and smooth occupancy across the weekend.

Our booking data show that weddings at Quayside Hall, the venue next door, account for around 38% of our Saturday-night room bookings. Wedding guests typically book as a block through the couple, arrive on the Saturday afternoon and check out on the Sunday morning.

5. Revenue impact
Across our 124 rooms, 104 weekend nights a year and average weekend occupancy of 79%, a £20 increase in BAR is worth about £204,000 a year in additional room revenue, before any gain from longer stays. We have assumed weekend occupancy is maintained at 2025 levels, which we consider prudent given the evidence above.

The two-night minimum should add further revenue through additional Friday and Sunday nights. We have not quantified this but expect it to be material, particularly in shoulder months.

6. Implementation and monitoring
The new rates will be loaded into the channel manager on 15 May for stays from 1 June, giving online travel agencies two weeks' notice. Corporate contracted rates and group rates already contracted will be honoured. We will review pick-up weekly against the same weeks in 2025 and report to the General Manager monthly. If weekend occupancy for any month falls more than five points below 2025, we will review the rate.

7. Recommendation
The evidence shows that our weekend guests are not price sensitive at current rates and that we are priced well below our competitive set. We recommend approval of the £165 weekend BAR and the two-night Saturday minimum from 1 June 2026, delivering at least £204,000 of additional annual room revenue.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [inconsistency] at: "Across our 124 rooms, 104 weekend nights a year and average weekend occupancy of 79%" -- The hotel is described as a 112-room hotel in the Context section, but the revenue estimate uses 124 rooms. With 112 rooms the same calculation gives 112 x 104 x 0.79 x £20 = about £184,000, not £204,000.
2. [unsupported_causal] at: "This tells us that our weekend guests are not price sensitive at current levels" -- The only evidence is that occupancy rose from June to July after a June rate rise, but the document itself says July and August are the strongest months because of the harbour festival and school holidays. The seasonal rise confounds the comparison; it cannot show demand is price-insensitive (let alone that the higher price helped).
3. [missing_consideration] at: "We have assumed weekend occupancy is maintained at 2025 levels, which we consider prudent given the evidence above." -- The document states that about 38% of Saturday-night bookings are wedding guests from the adjacent venue who stay only Saturday night. A two-night minimum would exclude or deter this group, but the revenue case assumes occupancy is maintained and never addresses the loss of these single-night Saturday bookings.

REVIEW:
# Review: Weekend Rate Restructure, Harbourside Hotel

**What the paper proposes.** From 1 June 2026, raise the Friday and Saturday Best Available Rate from £145 to £165, and require a two-night minimum for any stay that includes a Saturday. It claims at least £204,000 a year in extra revenue. Its evidence is the June 2025 rate rise, a value-for-money score of 8.4, and the hotel being priced £20–35 below competitors.

**Verdict.** There is a real case for charging more on peak weekends. Thirty-one Saturdays sold out in 2025, and the hotel is priced below its competitive set. But the paper's main evidence on price sensitivity doesn't show what it claims. The revenue figure uses the wrong room count and applies the increase to rooms that won't pay it. The two-night minimum is presented as pure upside, yet it clashes with 38% of the hotel's Saturday business. The £204,000 figure is not a floor.

---

## 1. What checks out

- **Average occupancy.** The monthly figures in Table 1 average 79.2%, matching the stated 79%.
- **Gap to competitors.** £145 is £20–35 below the £165–180 competitor range.
- **The arithmetic, on its own inputs.** 124 × 104 × 0.79 × £20 ≈ £203,800.
- **Signs of unmet demand on peak dates are real.** Thirty-one sold-out Saturdays and 89–93% occupancy in July and August show demand exceeding supply at the current price on those dates. That is legitimate support for higher peak pricing.

---

## 2. The June–July "test" is seasonality

The paper says occupancy rose from 81% in June to 89% in July after a £10 rise, so guests aren't price sensitive. But section 2 of the paper itself says July and August are the strongest months "driven by the harbour festival and the school summer holidays." The July jump is what the hotel would expect from the calendar whatever it charged. Occupancy kept rising into August (93%) and stayed high in September (88%), the normal seasonal pattern.

The comparison would need to be like for like: July 2025 against July 2024, or the first year at £145 against the year before. Even then, festival dates and economic conditions would muddy it.

The claim that the rise "reinforced our positioning as a quality option" is speculation, not a finding.

**The value-for-money score.** A score of 8.4 shows guests think the hotel is good value *at £145*. A higher price is likely to lower that score. The score shows there may be room to raise prices. It doesn't show guests won't respond to them.

---

## 3. The revenue estimate is overstated

**3a. Wrong room count.** Section 2 says the hotel has 112 rooms. The calculation uses 124. With 112 rooms the maximum is 112 × 104 × 0.79 × £20 ≈ **£184,000**.

**3b. Not every room pays the published rate.** The £20 is applied to every occupied weekend room-night. But:
- Corporate contracted rates and existing group rates will be honoured (section 6).
- Weddings are 38% of Saturday room bookings, booked as blocks, probably at negotiated group rates.

Only rooms sold at the published rate gain £20. If 30–40% of weekend room-nights are on other rates, the uplift falls to roughly **£110,000–130,000**. The real figure needs the hotel's breakdown of bookings by rate type.

**3c. Not all of the £20 reaches the hotel.** Online travel agencies typically take about 15–20% commission. UK hotel prices shown to guests usually include 20% VAT, so if £145 includes VAT, the hotel keeps about £16.67 of each £20 before commission. The paper should state whether its figures are gross or net.

**3d. "Occupancy maintained" is assumed, not prudent.** The evidence for it is the seasonal test in §2. The "conservative" label only covers the occupancy *gain* the author hoped for. It doesn't cover the possibility of losing bookings.

**Break-even.** Taking only rooms sold at the published rate, revenue per available room is £145 × 0.79 ≈ £114.55 today. At £165, occupancy can fall to about 69.4% before that revenue drops, about **10 points**. That is a reasonable margin, and the paper should have stated it. It ignores lost spending on food and drink, which shrinks the margin somewhat.

---

## 4. The two-night minimum works against the wedding business

This is the most serious problem, and the paper's own data show it.

- Weddings at Quayside Hall account for **38% of Saturday bookings**. Wedding guests arrive Saturday and leave Sunday morning.
- A minimum stay applied to "any stay that includes a Saturday night" would either turn these guests away or force them to pay for a night they won't use. Many would book elsewhere.
- Only *already contracted* group rates are protected. New wedding blocks for next season would be caught by the rule. This also puts the hotel's relationship with the venue next door at risk.

On Saturdays that don't sell out (about 21 of 52 in 2025), the rule turns away one-night guests with no two-night guest to replace them. That is lost revenue, not extra revenue. Hotels usually apply minimum stays only to dates expected to sell out, not every Saturday.

So the minimum stay is a risk to revenue that the paper doesn't quantify, not an "unquantified material" gain. It undermines "£204,000 is a floor": that floor assumes the two-night rule costs nothing. **Possible remedy:** apply the minimum only to dates expected to sell out, and exempt wedding blocks.

---

## 5. A flat rise vs date-based pricing

Weekend occupancy ranges from 62% in January to 93% in August. A flat £20 rise all year makes the most sense where demand already exceeds supply and the least sense in January and February. A more defensible proposal would:
- raise rates by date: higher from late spring to September and on Saturdays expected to sell out;
- hold or test in the low months;
- use the low months as a cleaner test of how guests respond to price, comparing against the same weeks in 2025.

At £165 the hotel matches the cheapest competitor rather than undercutting it. "Bringing pricing into line" is fair, but it changes the hotel's position in the market.

---

## 6. Monitoring

- **Good:** weekly pick-up against 2025 is the right approach. A 5-point trigger sits inside the roughly 10-point break-even margin.
- **It will react late.** Leisure guests book weeks ahead, so a *month's* occupancy reveals a problem only after many future nights are already priced. Watch booking pace for future dates, not past occupancy.
- **The trigger is vague.** "Review the rate" doesn't say what happens next. Decide in advance: for example, return to £155 for affected dates.
- **The minimum stay isn't monitored at all.** Track Saturday occupancy separately, wedding block enquiries and losses, and turned-away one-night requests.

---

## 7. Summary of corrections

| Claim | Status |
|---|---|
| Guests not price sensitive (June–July test) | **Not supported.** The rise matches the seasonal pattern. |
| Priced £20–35 below competitors | Correct |
| £204,000 extra revenue | **Overstated.** About £184,000 maximum with 112 rooms; roughly £110,000–130,000 once contracted, group and wedding rates are excluded; lower again after commission and VAT if quoted gross |
| £204,000 is a floor | **No.** It assumes no lost bookings, and the minimum stay can reduce revenue |
| Minimum stay adds revenue | **Open, with clear downside risk.** It conflicts with 38% of Saturday business |
| Corporate and group protected | Only *already contracted* business |

## Bottom line

- **The rate rise.** Some increase is probably justified, given sold-out Saturdays, strong summer occupancy and pricing below competitors. Do it by date, starting with peak periods. Present a revenue range with stated assumptions, not a floor.
- **The two-night minimum.** Don't apply it to every Saturday. Restrict it to dates expected to sell out and exempt wedding blocks, or drop it.
- **Still open.** How guests respond to price. The real answer will come from comparing booking pace in the low months against the same weeks in 2025.
